A1.justification: Both PDFs describe the same authors' moment-constrained optimal transport framework despite substantial retitling and refocusing. All 20 pages of v1 and 23 pages of v2, including their appendices, support comparison.

before.justification: V1 contains theoretical results, computational proposals, and analytical Gaussian and stochastic-control examples. Neither the main text nor the appendix reports original experimental or simulation outcomes.

after.justification: V2 reports original EV-charging simulations, runtime comparisons, an ElaadNL data-based scheduling study, prediction-error experiments, and numerical transport experiments in Appendix D.

M1.justification: V2 extends the retained entropic moment-transport framework into MCOT-C with inequality constraints and explicit preservation of exogenous coordinates. It introduces projected Semi-Sinkhorn updates, a Newton option, and online reoptimization with sampled charging decisions. V1's soft-penalty formulation and detailed Monte Carlo/Zap procedures are no longer developed.

E1.justification: V1 has no empirical dataset or evaluated task coverage. V2 adds simulated EV charging, online scheduling using ElaadNL weekday transactions, charging-interruption and inaccurate-forecast scenarios, and numerical transport from a uniform distribution in Appendix D.

E2.justification: V2 introduces evaluated comparisons absent from v1: PDMP for computation time in Figure 4 and IOCS, modified to control plugging times, for vehicle acceptance in Section 4.7 and Figure 7. It also evaluates the nominal Plug When Arrive strategy.

E3.justification: V2 introduces experimental protocols, including a nominal 90/10 weekday split, discretized online evaluation, and a runtime comparison with all vehicles arriving at 9am to accommodate PDMP. The IOCS comparison imposes a strict 650 kW cap and measures rejected vehicles. These are new evaluations, not revisions of v1 experiments; v2 inconsistently states the test size and slope constraint.

E4.justification: V2 adds comparisons with and without charging interruption and consumption-slope constraints, a forecast stress test changing predicted arrivals by 30%, and an Appendix D regularization sweep from 10^-3 to 10^3. These investigate flexibility, forecast robustness, and regularization effects; v1 contains no corresponding empirical analyses.

E5.justification: Figure 4 in v2 introduces PDMP runtime error bars computed over 10 simulations, without specifying their statistical definition. V1 reports no empirical uncertainty or repeated-run counts. This is new reporting, not evidence of an increased run count.

E6.justification: V2 adds all empirical findings: Figure 4 reports MCOT faster than PDMP, and Section 4.7 reports 23 rejected vehicles (3.4%) for MCOT versus 33 (4.9%) for modified IOCS under the same cap. Section 4.6 reports charging delay increasing from 11 to 12 minutes with poorer forecasts. These are new results, not performance improvements over v1 measurements.

T1.justification: V2 reformulates duality for inequalities and restricted control kernels, adds an online error bound in Proposition 3, and adds a regularization-value bound and derivation in Proposition 6 and Appendix B. It removes the soft-penalty dual and v1's Gaussian joint-covariance and explicit optimizer results. The Gaussian conditional kernel and Markov factorization are retained in Appendices B–C.

C1.justification: V1 foregrounds general OT relaxations, finite-dimensional dual characterization, soft penalties, and Monte Carlo computation. V2 foregrounds mean-field control, hard agent constraints, a Semi-Sinkhorn solver, online EV scheduling, and computational advantages. This substantially changes the scope of the headline contributions while retaining the central moment-relaxation idea.

C2.justification: V2 adds substantive explanations of charging priorities, rebound peaks, and robustness through rescheduling unconnected vehicles. It attributes constraint overshoots to unexpected arrivals, exhausted flexibility, and solver tolerance, and introduces a no-outlier assumption and state-space scaling limitations. V1 instead emphasizes potentially infeasible moment classes and general computational prospects.

D1.justification: V2 adds solver and online pseudocode, discretization sizes, regularization values, power bins, data preparation, and an explicit stopping criterion. Its reproducibility statement newly says code and data accompany supplementary material, although their availability cannot be verified from the supplied PDFs. V1 has mathematical computational instructions but no comparable empirical implementation documentation.

R1.justification: V2 substantially repositions the work around mean-field control and EV scheduling, adding discussions of Alfonsi's moment relaxation, unbalanced OT, PDMP, IOCS, and EV datasets. V1's historical moment-problem, mismatched-decoding, and broader relaxation positioning is substantially reduced, with numerous associated references removed.

P1.justification: The title, abstract, introduction, contribution statement, and conclusion are extensively rewritten around control applications. The main narrative becomes model, algorithm, simulated EV charging, and online evaluation; much of the earlier theoretical exposition moves into reorganized Appendices A–C.

P2.justification: V1's single geometry diagram is revised and relocated as Figure 8. V2 adds nine empirical figures and two algorithm displays, with extensive changes to typography and text wrapping. Visual inspection also reveals overlapping text around Algorithm 1 and between Figure 9's caption and the adjacent derivation.

improvement.justification: V2 adds substantial practical support through an online solver, real-data comparisons, and robustness tests. However, its revised dual in Equation 8 conflicts with the gradient sign in Proposition 2, and Appendix D derives its reference optimum without enforcing the stated interval constraint. Conflicting test counts (674 versus 713) and slope limits (100 versus 120 kW/h) further weaken verification. These material reliability problems prevent a confident net-quality judgment despite the practical gains.
